Assuming Postgres and a `users` table (no schema to check here, so adjust the names). I have not run this against a database.

```sql
BEGIN;

ALTER TABLE users
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS first_name text,
  ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS last_name  text;

-- ponytail: naive split, first word = first_name, rest = last_name ("Mary Ann Smith" -> "Mary" / "Ann Smith")
-- ponytail: single UPDATE locks every row it touches; batch by id range if the table is large
UPDATE users
SET first_name = substring(btrim(full_name) from '^\S+'),
    last_name  = NULLIF(regexp_replace(btrim(full_name), '^\S+\s*', ''), '')
WHERE full_name IS NOT NULL
  AND first_name IS NULL
  AND last_name IS NULL;

COMMIT;

-- check: should return 0
SELECT count(*) FROM users
WHERE btrim(full_name) <> '' AND first_name IS NULL;
```

It is safe to run twice because `ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` is a no-op the second time, and the `WHERE ... IS NULL` guard means the backfill only touches rows that have not been split. A rerun will not overwrite names that were edited after the first run.

Single-word names get a `NULL` `last_name`.

Skipped: dropping `full_name`. Do that in a separate migration (`DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS`) once nothing reads or writes it, since it is the only irreversible step.
